lead: Hooke's law says that inside the elastic limit, stress grows in direct proportion to strain. The constant is Young's modulus E for tension or shear modulus G for shear. Real designs do not run at the failure stress. Engineers divide a chosen failure stress by a factor of safety n to get an allowable stress, also called working stress. The safe load follows from this stress and the cross-section area. Tie rods, bolts, shafts and pressure parts use this pair of ideas every day.

sections.h3: Hooke's law for tension and shear

blocks.text: Hooke's law is the linear part of the stress-strain curve from Chapter 1.2. For a bar in axial tension, σ = E ε. σ is normal stress in Pa, equal to P/A; ε is axial strain, equal to ΔL/L and dimensionless; E is Young's modulus in Pa, often quoted in GPa. The law holds only within the elastic limit. Below that limit, unloading returns the bar to its original length. Above the limit, permanent strain remains and the straight line no longer applies.

blocks.where: σ is normal stress (Pa, or N/mm² = MPa); E is Young's modulus (Pa); ε is axial strain (dimensionless).

blocks.text: In shear, the same linear idea uses τ = G γ. τ is shear stress in Pa; γ is shear strain in radians; G is the shear modulus, also called modulus of rigidity, in Pa. G is smaller than E for the same metal. Typical steel has E near 200 GPa and G near 80 GPa. Chapter 1.4 relates E, G and Poisson's ratio.

blocks.where: τ is shear stress (Pa); G is shear modulus or modulus of rigidity (Pa); γ is shear strain (rad).

sections.h3: Factor of safety and working stress

blocks.text: No useful design sets σ equal to the stress that breaks or yields the material. The factor of safety n compares a failure stress σ<sub>f</sub> with the stress allowed in service σ<sub>w</sub>. σ<sub>f</sub> is a material strength: yield strength σ<sub>y</sub> for a ductile metal, ultimate strength σ<sub>u</sub> for a brittle material. σ<sub>w</sub> is the allowable, working or permissible stress. n is dimensionless and greater than 1.
n = σ<sub>f</sub> / σ<sub>w</sub>   so   σ<sub>w</sub> = σ<sub>f</sub> / n
blocks.where: n is factor of safety (dimensionless); σ<sub>f</sub> is failure stress (Pa); σ<sub>w</sub> is working, allowable or permissible stress (Pa).

blocks.text: For an axial member of area A, the safe load is P = σ<sub>w</sub> A. P is in N when σ<sub>w</sub> is in N/mm² and A in mm². In shear, replace σ by τ and use the shear strength or shear yield strength. The same factor may be applied to shear stress: τ<sub>w</sub> = τ<sub>f</sub> / n.

blocks.where: P is safe axial load (N); σ<sub>w</sub> is working stress (Pa); A is cross-section area (m² or mm²); σ<sub>f</sub> is failure stress (Pa); n is factor of safety.

sections.h3: Choosing the failure stress and the factor

blocks.text: The choice of σ<sub>f</sub> follows the material and the design rule. Ductile materials such as mild steel show a clear yield point. A design based on yield prevents permanent stretch. Brittle materials such as cast iron break with little warning. Their design often uses ultimate strength. Some design rules use a proof stress for materials without a clear yield point. The factor n is then chosen for the job, not copied as a universal number.

items: Loads may be larger than the estimate: overload, vibration, wind, or a Chennai power cut that starts a pump against a closed valve.
Material strength varies from batch to batch and with temperature, work hardening and corrosion.
Analysis is simplified: joints are not perfectly pinned, loads are not exactly axial, and stress concentrations are ignored in a first check.
Failure has different costs: a toy bracket and an IRCTC bridge do not carry the same consequence.
Inspection and maintenance are imperfect, so a margin covers wear and unnoticed damage.

blocks.text: No single universal FOS value exists. Codes, company rules and the consequence of failure set it. A mild steel tie rod with σ<sub>y</sub> = 250 MPa and n = 2.5 has σ<sub>w</sub> = 100 MPa. The figure follows that chain from failure stress to safe load. The worked example uses a 12 mm rod.

figure.caption: The rod's yield strength 250 MPa is divided by 2.5 to give 100 MPa, and the 12 mm area turns that into a safe load of 11.31 kN.

spec.title: Factor of safety
spec.aria: The failure stress is divided by the factor of safety to give the working stress, which sets the safe axial load.

examples.question: A mild steel tie rod has yield strength 250 MPa. The design uses a factor of safety 2.5. The rod diameter is 12 mm. Find the allowable stress and the maximum axial load for the rod.
steps: Design failure stress: σ<sub>f</sub> = σ<sub>y</sub> = 250 MPa = 250 N/mm².
Working stress: σ<sub>w</sub> = σ<sub>f</sub> / n = 250 / 2.5 = 100 MPa = 100 N/mm².
Cross-section area: A = π/4 × d² = π/4 × (12 mm)² = 0.7854 × 144 mm² = 113.1 mm².
Safe load: P = σ<sub>w</sub> A = 100 N/mm² × 113.1 mm² = 11310 N.
examples.answer: The allowable stress is 100 MPa and the maximum safe axial load is 11.31 kN.
examples.check:
import math
sigma_y = 250.0
n = 2.5
sigma_w = sigma_y / n
d = 12.0
A = math.pi / 4.0 * d**2
P = sigma_w * A
print(round(sigma_w, 1))
print(round(A, 1))
print(round(P / 1000.0, 2))

traps: Do not mix MPa and Pa. 1 MPa = 1 N/mm² = 10⁶ Pa. A stress of 250 MPa is 250 N/mm².
For a ductile rod, design usually uses yield strength, not ultimate strength. Ultimate is higher and hides yielding.
The factor of safety is dimensionless and greater than 1. A value like 2.5 is not 2.5 MPa.
Apply the factor to the failure stress to get working stress. When checking a given load, compare σ = P/A with σ<sub>w</sub>. Do not replace σ by P/(nA) and call it safe.
Shear uses G and τ = Gγ in the elastic range, not E and ε. The two moduli are different.

quiz.q: State Hooke's law in tension and give its formula.
quiz.a: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain. The formula is σ = Eε, where σ is normal stress, E is Young's modulus and ε is axial strain.

quiz.q: Define factor of safety and working stress.
quiz.a: Factor of safety n = failure stress / allowable stress. Working stress, also called allowable or permissible stress, is the stress allowed in service: σ<sub>w</sub> = σ<sub>f</sub>/n.

quiz.q: Why is a factor of safety needed even when Hooke's law is exact in the elastic range?
quiz.a: Hooke's law describes material response only. A factor of safety covers load uncertainty, material variation, simplified analysis, wear and the consequences of failure.

quiz.q: A steel has yield strength 320 MPa. The factor of safety is 4. Find the working stress.
A material has shear yield strength 120 MPa. Use a factor of safety 3 and a shear area of 500 mm². Find the allowable shear stress and the safe shear force.
quiz.a: τ<sub>w</sub> = 120/3 = 40 MPa = 40 N/mm². V = τ<sub>w</sub>A = 40 × 500 = 20000 N = 20 kN.

quiz.q: Why use ultimate strength for a brittle material but yield strength for a ductile material?
quiz.a: A ductile material yields and deforms permanently before breaking, so yielding is treated as failure. A brittle material has no clear yield and breaks suddenly, so ultimate strength is the available failure measure.

quiz.q: A student checks safety by comparing P/n with σ<sub>f</sub>A. Explain the error.
quiz.a: The factor of safety is applied to the failure stress, not to the applied load in the stress check. The safe condition is P/A ≤ σ<sub>f</sub>/n, or P ≤ σ<sub>f</sub>A/n. Comparing P/n with σ<sub>f</sub>A can pass a load larger than the safe load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern design codes replace a single FOS with partial factors on load and material strength, as in limit state design. Reliability methods treat strength and load as random variables and compute a probability of failure. Fatigue and fracture mechanics use separate factors for repeated loads or cracked members. Search next for limit state design, partial safety factor, reliability-based design and fatigue factor of safety.
